_README: Every iGEM Toronto season, 2005-2026. Drives the home page timeline, /history/, and one page per year at /history/<year>/. Transcribed from the alumni dataset (iGEM roster API + team wikis) documented in docs/HISTORY_AND_GALLERY.md. Deliberately contains NO personal names - see that doc for why and for where the names live. `medal: null` means no result is recorded, which is NOT the same as no medal; use the `note` field to say why. 2020 is absent because there was no Toronto team that year; the site renders that gap explicitly.

skippedYears.reason: iGEM ran a remote competition in 2020. Toronto did not enter.

years.project: PetaBite — PETase discovery from the Logan petabase index
years.blurb: Mining the Logan petabase index — a search across the entire public sequencing archive — for new plastic-degrading PETase enzymes.
years.story: PetaBite searches the Logan petabase index, a compressed representation of essentially every public sequencing run ever deposited, for enzymes that break down PET plastic. Where a conventional screen tests a handful of candidates, the index makes it possible to look across the whole archive at once. The season is still running; 66 members make it the second-largest team the chapter has fielded.
years.note: Current season. The wiki is still being built.

years.project: PHORAGER — Phage Host-Optimized Receptor-Activated Generative Engineering Repository
years.blurb: A generative pipeline for engineering bacteriophages against specific bacterial hosts, and the chapter's second consecutive Top 10 finish.
years.story: PHORAGER built a repository and generative design pipeline for retargeting bacteriophages at chosen bacterial hosts — an approach to infections that antibiotics no longer clear. The project won Best Therapeutics Project outright, was nominated for Best Model, and placed in the Top 10 of the overgraduate section, back to back with 2024.

years.blurb: Machine-learning-guided plasmid design aimed at antibiotic-resistant infections. The largest team in chapter history, and its first Top 10.
years.story: Plasmid.AI applied machine learning to plasmid design, with antibiotic-resistant infection as the target application. Against more than 400 teams from 48 countries, it took Gold, won both Best Model and Best Entrepreneurship, and placed in the Top 10 of the overgraduate section — the chapter's best result to that point. At 67 members it remains the largest team iGEM Toronto has fielded, and it was the first year the chapter ran a formal entrepreneurship division, which went on to compete in the U of T Entrepreneurship Hatchery's Demo Week.

years.project: Biological methane capture at landfill sites
years.blurb: Engineering methanotrophs to capture methane escaping from landfill sites, and five award nominations on top of a Best Model win.
years.story: Landfills leak methane, a greenhouse gas roughly eighty times more potent than CO2 over twenty years. Methanivore engineered methane-oxidising bacteria to capture it at the source. The project won Best Model and picked up five further nominations — Climate Crisis, Integrated Human Practices, Entrepreneurship, Presentation, and Wiki — the widest spread of nominations in chapter history.

years.project: Oak wilt fungal DNA detection by LAMP
years.blurb: A field-usable LAMP assay letting foresters detect oak wilt infection early enough to slow its spread.
years.story: Oak wilt, caused by the fungus Bretziella fagacearum, kills oaks faster than foresters can identify which trees are infected. The team built an on-site diagnostic using loop-mediated isothermal amplification, which needs no thermocycler and can run in the field. Presented at the Giant Jamboree in Paris alongside 346 teams from 45 countries; nominated for Best Conservation Project.

years.project: Computational enzyme design for PET-degrading enzymes
years.blurb: A fifteen-person software-track team that competed through the pandemic. The wiki was never filled in, so for years the project was assumed lost — it was recovered in 2026 from a surviving slide deck.
years.story:
2021 is often assumed to be a blank year. It was not: the iGEM roster records a full fifteen-person team in the Software track, and the wiki was left as the unedited iGEM template, which is why the project vanished from the record.

It was recovered in 2026 from a presentation given to BioZone in April 2021. The team was doing computational enzyme design for PET-degrading enzymes: building a probability distribution over plastic-degrading enzymes, expanding sequence space with ProteinSolver, running a Rosetta design pipeline, and closing a dry-lab/wet-lab active-learning loop with a Gaussian process trained on 25 million sequences. The deck cites the 2019 team’s BioBrick parts as prior work, which makes 2019 and 2021 one continuous line rather than two separate attempts.

It is also the closest ancestor of the 2026 project. PetaBite is making structurally the same bet — machine-learning-guided discovery of better PETases — five years later and at a very different scale.
years.note: Project recovered in 2026 from a BioZone slide deck, not the wiki. The 2021 wiki remains the unedited iGEM template.

years.project: Accelerating industrial plastic degradation with PETase
years.blurb: Engineering PETase to break down industrial plastic waste faster — the chapter's first gold since 2013.
years.story: The team engineered the enzyme PETase to accelerate the breakdown of PET plastic waste, taking Gold at the Giant Jamboree in Boston — the first since 2013 — and a Best Manufacturing Project nomination that placed the project in the top five of its track. Seven years later the 2026 team returned to PETase from a completely different direction, searching the public sequencing archive for better variants rather than engineering a known one.

years.project: Flotation, Separation, Bio-remediation (E. coli gas vesicle proteins)
years.blurb: Using bacterial gas vesicle proteins to float contaminants out of water for separation and remediation.
years.story: The team expressed gas vesicle proteins in E. coli so that cells bound to a contaminant would float, making separation a matter of skimming rather than filtration. Silver medal. The team and description pages of the wiki were left as templates, so the project name here is recovered from the site banner rather than from a project description.
years.note: The wiki's Team and Description pages were never filled in.

years.blurb: A light-switchable transcription factor, fusing the LacI repressor to the LOV photosensory domain.
years.story: LacILOV fused the LacI repressor to a LOV light-sensing domain, giving a transcription factor that can be switched with light instead of a chemical inducer — finer control in both time and space than IPTG allows. Bronze medal.

years.blurb: A paper strip that changes colour in the presence of gold ions, built on the GolS gold-sensing regulator.
years.story: Built around GolS, a bacterial transcriptional regulator that responds to gold ions, the team developed a paper-based colorimetric test for gold in solution — cheap, field-deployable detection with no instrument required. Bronze medal, from a 51-person team.

years.blurb: Flux balance analysis extended from single organisms to whole microbial consortia.
years.story: Flux balance analysis models the metabolism of one organism well and a community of them badly. ConsortiaFlux extended the method to microbial consortia, where organisms exchange metabolites. Silver medal and a Best Applied Design nomination.

years.blurb: Keeping engineered organisms from surviving outside the environment they were designed for.
years.story: Any engineered organism intended for release needs a way to fail safely outside its intended setting. The team proposed a biocontainment strategy to prevent engineered E. coli from persisting in the wild. Bronze medal.

years.project: A Systems Biology Approach to Biofilm Engineering
years.blurb: The chapter's first gold medal — modelling and engineering biofilm formation as a system rather than a single pathway.
years.story: A sixteen-person team took the chapter's first Gold, treating biofilm formation as a network problem and combining modelling with wet lab work to engineer it. It stood as the only Toronto gold for six years, until 2019.

years.blurb: A two-part project in Arabidopsis, run by the smallest team the chapter has ever entered.
years.story: Ten people — the smallest iGEM Toronto team on record — entered a two-part Arabidopsis engineering project in the Food & Energy track. No results page survives for 2012, so the competition outcome is unknown rather than absent.
years.note: No result recorded: no reachable iGEM results page exists for this year.

years.blurb: A twelve-person New Application team whose project description was never written to the wiki.
years.story: The roster records twelve members entered in the New Application track, but the project wiki was left as the unedited iGEM template — down to the placeholder line about writing your abstract here. Neither the project name nor the results are recoverable from any surviving source.
years.note: Project unrecoverable — the wiki was left as the iGEM template. No result recorded either.

years.project: Oil sands tailings bioremediation via catechol metabolic channeling
years.blurb: Metabolic channeling of catechol, aimed at cleaning up Alberta oil sands tailings ponds.
years.story: The team designed a catechol-degrading pathway using metabolic channeling — physically co-locating successive enzymes so intermediates never diffuse away — for bioremediation of oil sands tailings. No results page survives for 2010.
years.note: No result recorded: no reachable iGEM results page exists for this year.

years.blurb: The team's return after the 2008 withdrawal, reorganised around the Parkinson lab at MaRS.
years.story: After 2008 fell through, the team reorganised inside the Parkinson lab at the MaRS Discovery District and entered as TorontoMaRSDiscovery. The Encapsulator took Bronze — the first medal the chapter had won since 2007.

years.blurb: Registered, then withdrew. Only three people ever joined the roster.
years.story: 2008 is the one season the chapter registered and did not compete. Three people joined the roster and the team withdrew before the Jamboree, while it was reorganising into the Parkinson lab at MaRS — the arrangement it returned under in 2009.
years.note: Registered then withdrew. No competition result exists because the team did not compete.

years.blurb: A neural network built out of communicating bacteria — the chapter's first medal.
years.story: Competing as BlueGenes, the team built a bacterial neural network: cells wired into a simple computational circuit through intercellular signalling. It won Silver, the chapter's first medal. Note that iGEM's own awards API does not list this result; it is confirmed directly from the 2007 results page.
years.note: Silver confirmed from 2007.igem.org/Results. iGEM's awards API has no record of it.

years.blurb: Year two of the joint Toronto–Waterloo Blue Water team, forty-three members strong.
years.story: Blue Water returned for a second year on the Cell-See-Us Thermometer with forty-three people on the roster — a size the chapter would not match again for a decade. The wiki from this year is the only one that still carries student contact details, published by the members themselves. No results page survives for 2006.
years.note: No result recorded: no reachable iGEM results page exists for this year.

years.blurb: Where it starts: a joint University of Toronto and University of Waterloo team called Blue Water.
years.story: The first season. Toronto entered jointly with the University of Waterloo under the name Blue Water, thirteen people building a cellular thermometer — bacteria engineered to report temperature. No images from this year survive; the wiki hotlinked a personal university page that has long since gone. No results page survives either.
years.note: No result recorded: no reachable iGEM results page exists for this year.
